course: CMU 21-254: Linear Algebra and Vector Calculus for Engineers
audience: SI leader teaching live on a whiteboard. This is not a student worksheet.
toneRule: Keep explanations very simple, verbal, and board-friendly. Avoid textbook phrasing unless the problem needs it.
title: Curves, Tangent Vectors, and Arc Length
sessionGoal: Students should be able to read a parametrized curve, find velocity/speed/unit tangent, parametrize a line segment, and compute simple arc length.
quickStartIfUnprepared: Start with the sentence: a parametrized curve is a moving point.
Do Problem 1 to review position, velocity, speed, and unit tangent.
Do Problem 2 if students struggle with parametrizing segments.
Do Problem 3 to show a clean arc length example.
sayThisFirst: A curve \(r(t)\) is a position that changes with time.
\(r'(t)\) is the velocity vector, so it points tangent to the curve.
Speed is the length of velocity: \(\|r'(t)\|\).
Arc length adds up speed over the interval.
boardPlan: Write position, velocity, speed, unit tangent.
Show line segment parametrization from A to B.
Finish with one arc length integral where speed is constant.
keyFormulas: Line segment from A to B: \(r(t)=A+t(B-A),\ 0\le t\le1\).
commonMistakes: Forgetting that velocity is a vector but speed is a number.
Using \(A-B\) instead of \(B-A\) for a segment from A to B.
Forgetting the interval for a parametrization.
Integrating \(r(t)\) instead of \(\|r'(t)\|\) for arc length.
notationWarnings: Use \(\overrightarrow{AB}=B-A\) for the vector from A to B.
The unit tangent only exists when \(r'(t)\ne 0\).

problems.title: Position, velocity, speed, and unit tangent
problems.studentPromptLatex: Let \(r(t)=(t^2,t^3-3t,2t)\). Find \(r(1)\), \(r'(1)\), the speed at \(t=1\), and the unit tangent vector at \(t=1\).
problems.whatToSayBefore: Say: take the derivative component-by-component. Then speed is just the length of that derivative vector.

drawInstructions: Draw a curve in 3D or as a simple squiggle.
Draw an arrow tangent to the curve labeled r'(1).
Label speed as the length of r'(1), not a new direction.

walkthrough.label: Divide by speed to get the unit tangent

commonMistakes: Calling \(r'(1)\) the speed. \(r'(1)\) is velocity; its magnitude is speed.
Forgetting to divide by the speed for the unit tangent.

practiceLabPointer.note: Practice Lab Section 7 for curves and tangent vectors.

problems.title: Parametrize a line segment
problems.studentPromptLatex: Parametrize the line segment from \(A=(1,2,0)\) to \(B=(4,-1,3)\). Then find its length.
problems.whatToSayBefore: Say: start at A, then add t times the vector from A to B.

drawInstructions: Draw point A and point B.
Draw an arrow from A to B.
Show t=0 gives A and t=1 gives B.

walkthrough.label: Find the length
walkthrough.latex: The length of the segment is \[\|\overrightarrow{AB}\|=\sqrt{3^2+(-3)^2+3^2}=\sqrt{27}=3\sqrt3.\]

commonMistakes: Writing a line instead of a line segment.

practiceLabPointer.note: Practice Lab Section 7 for parametrized curves.

problems.title: Arc length of a helix
problems.studentPromptLatex: Find the arc length of \(r(t)=(3\cos t,3\sin t,4t)\) for \(0\le t\le2\pi\).
problems.whatToSayBefore: Say: arc length is not about the position vector. It is the integral of speed.

drawInstructions: Draw a helix wrapping upward around the z-axis.
Draw a tangent arrow and label its length as 5.
Explain that constant speed makes the integral easy.

commonMistakes: Integrating each component separately instead of speed.
Dropping the vertical component \(4t\), which changes the length.

practiceLabPointer.note: Practice Lab Section 7 for arc length.

wrapUpQuestions: What is the difference between velocity and speed?
How do you parametrize from A to B?

Checked line segment direction and length.
Checked helix speed is constant 5 and length is 10pi.
reviewSummary: Session 16 is ready with exact visual specs for curve tangent, segment, and helix sketches.

open.title: A curve is a trip
say: Welcome to the calculus half of the course. We start with the simplest moving object: a point traveling along a curve.
r(t) is where you are at time t. Its derivative is your velocity: which way you're going and how fast. Everything today is built from those two ideas.

ask.q: You drive around a roundabout at a steady 20 mph. Is your velocity constant?
ask.a: No. Your speed is constant, but your direction keeps changing, so velocity changes.

idea.title: Velocity is a vector, speed is its length
say: Differentiate r(t) one component at a time and you get the velocity vector r′(t). Put its tail on the curve and it points along the curve, in the direction of travel.
Its length is the speed. Divide the velocity by the speed and you get T, the unit tangent: pure direction, length 1.
Arc length is the odometer: add up speed over time. Speed × time = distance, with an integral when the speed changes.
draw: Draw a wavy curve with a dot on it labeled r(t), and an arrow from the dot along the curve labeled r′(t).
Draw a short arrow on top of it labeled T (length 1).

ask.q: Can the speed ever be negative?

launch.say: At t = 1, find the position, the velocity, the speed and the unit tangent.
circulate: Check every component was differentiated, including 2t → 2.
Speed is a number; velocity and T are vectors. Ask students to label each.

askFirst.q: Which of the four answers are vectors?
askFirst.a: Position, velocity and T are vectors; speed is a number.

ask.q: Is this a point or a direction?
ask.a: A point: where the traveler is at t = 1.

steps.say: Differentiate each component: r′(t) = (2t, 3t² − 3, 2), so r′(1) = (2, 0, 2).

ask.q: The y-velocity is 0 at t = 1. What does that mean?
ask.a: y is momentarily not changing: y = t³ − 3t has a turning point at t = 1.
Speed is the length of the velocity vector, not the sum of its entries.

steps.why: T strips away how fast you're going and keeps only which way.

si16-p1.meaning: At t = 1 the traveler is at (1, −2, 2), moving at 2√2 units per second, heading diagonally in the x–z direction with no y-motion at that instant.

ifStuck.if: a student reports r′(1) as the speed
ifStuck.then: ask whether the answer should be a vector or a number.

si16-p1.transition: That curve was given. Next, you build one: the straight-line trip between two points.

launch.say: Parametrize the segment from A to B, then find its length.
circulate: Check B − A, not A − B.
Does everyone have the interval 0 ≤ t ≤ 1?

askFirst.q: Where should the traveler be at t = 0? At t = 1?

steps.say: The trip's direction is B − A = (3, −3, 3).

ask.q: What does A − B describe instead?
ask.a: The trip from B back to A.

steps.say: Start at A and add t copies of B − A: r(t) = (1 + 3t, 2 − 3t, 3t) for 0 ≤ t ≤ 1.
steps.why: The interval is what makes it a segment. Without it, r(t) describes the whole infinite line.

ask.q: How does this match the arc length formula?
ask.a: Speed is |r′(t)| = √27, constant, over 1 unit of time: ∫₀¹ √27 dt = 3√3.

si16-p2.meaning: A straight trip at constant velocity: every second of t covers the whole vector B − A, so the length is just its magnitude.

ifStuck.if: a student's parametrization ends at the wrong point
ifStuck.then: plug in t = 0 and t = 1 and compare with A and B.

si16-p2.transition: Last one: a curve that isn't straight, but whose speed turns out to be constant anyway.

launch.say: Find the length of one full turn of the helix.
circulate: Is anyone integrating r(t) itself? Redirect to speed.
Look for sin² + cos² = 1 in their work.

askFirst.q: What do we integrate for arc length: position, velocity or speed?

ask.q: Which part of the motion is the 4?
ask.a: The steady climb up the z-axis.

steps.say: Speed² = 9 sin²t + 9 cos²t + 16 = 9 + 16 = 25, so the speed is 5, always.

ask.q: Why does the speed come out constant?
ask.a: The helix circles at a steady rate and climbs at a steady rate.

steps.why: sin² + cos² = 1 is the reason almost every circle and helix problem has a clean answer.

steps.say: Constant speed 5 for a time of 2π: L = 5 · 2π = 10π.

ask.q: Unroll one turn of the helix onto paper. What shape is it?
ask.a: A right triangle: base 6π (the circle), height 8π (the climb), hypotenuse 10π. A 3-4-5 triangle!

si16-p3.meaning: One turn of the helix covers 6π around and 8π up. Unrolled, it's the hypotenuse of a 3-4-5 triangle, 10π long.

ifStuck.then: ask whether the climb in z adds any distance.

wrap.write: Velocity r′(t): a vector along the curve. Speed |r′(t)|: a number. Segment A → B: A + t(B − A), 0 ≤ t ≤ 1. Arc length: integrate speed.

exit.a: Velocity is a vector with direction; speed is its length.
Distance = speed × time, added up with an integral.

wrap.next: Next session: functions of two variables, level curves and partial derivatives.
